title: Bronchiectasis: Confirm the Pattern, Find the Cause, Prevent Exacerbations
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic airway dilatation with impaired mucus clearance and recurrent infection/inflammation. Confirm the diagnosis with appropriate chest imaging, identify treatable causes, obtain sputum microbiology during clinically meaningful exacerbations, and build long-term airway-clearance and prevention plans rather than repeatedly prescribing empiric antibiotics without reassessment.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, daily sputum, hemoptysis, crackles and progressive exertional limitation are common clues.
Exacerbation is a clinical deterioration in respiratory symptoms and sputum burden rather than a positive culture alone.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist but do not explain structural bronchial dilatation by themselves.
Cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspiration, prior severe infection and ciliary disorders are among important etiologic categories.
Colonization is not the same as acute infection; prior sputum organisms help guide treatment when the patient actually exacerbates.
assessment: Ask about childhood/recurrent infections, aspiration/reflux, autoimmune disease, sinus disease, infertility history, immune problems, hemoptysis, exacerbation frequency and prior resistant organisms.
Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, sputum quantity/colour, fever, focal findings and whether hemoptysis or sepsis makes the episode urgent.
workup: High-resolution chest CT confirms the structural diagnosis when clinically appropriate.
Obtain sputum culture during significant exacerbation and review prior microbiology; test for underlying causes selectively rather than ordering an indiscriminate panel.
Spirometry helps characterize airflow limitation and comorbid obstructive disease but does not establish bronchiectasis alone.
management: Teach and reinforce individualized airway-clearance techniques, exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation where appropriate, vaccination and smoking cessation.

Treat exacerbations with antibiotics guided by prior/current microbiology and severity when bacterial infection is clinically likely; reassess if response is poor and consider source/complication issues.
Frequent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas or complex disease warrants respirology-directed prevention strategy.
medicationSafety: Long-term macrolide or inhaled antibiotic strategies require specialist-level indication review, resistance/QT/hearing or drug-specific monitoring rather than automatic chronic prescribing.
Bronchodilator or inhaled corticosteroid use should be driven by coexisting asthma/COPD or another supported indication, not bronchiectasis diagnosis alone.
redFlags: New focal chest pain with pneumothorax concern
counselling: Teach daily airway-clearance adherence, hydration, vaccination and when a change in sputum/respiratory status should trigger reassessment.
Explain that repeated antibiotics without cultures or an exacerbation phenotype can increase resistance without improving the underlying clearance problem.
followUp: Track exacerbation frequency, sputum microbiology, lung function, nutrition/weight and functional status.
Refer or co-manage with respirology when disease is frequent, severe, etiologically unclear or associated with resistant organisms.
examTrap: Treating every positive sputum culture as an acute infection or giving inhaled corticosteroid solely because bronchiectasis is present.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is airway clearance plus cause finding plus microbiology-guided exacerbation treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory guideline library and Non-CF Bronchiectasis working-group resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize the Syndrome and Refer by Cause
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes. Suspect it in unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart findings, use echocardiography to estimate probability and evaluate structure, search for common cardiac/lung/thromboembolic causes, and refer suspected pulmonary arterial or chronic thromboembolic disease for specialist confirmation and treatment rather than starting targeted vasodilators empirically.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, exertional chest discomfort, syncope/presyncope, edema, elevated JVP and a loud pulmonic component can occur.
Right-heart failure is a late/high-risk presentation and may be worsened by pregnancy or acute illness.
differentiate: Left-heart disease and chronic lung disease are common causes of elevated pulmonary pressures and require treatment of the underlying condition.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension is potentially treatable and should be considered after prior PE or unexplained PH.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension requires invasive hemodynamic confirmation before disease-specific treatment.
assessment: Assess functional limitation, syncope, chest pain, edema, oxygenation, connective-tissue disease features, liver disease, HIV risk, stimulant/anorexigen exposure, VTE history, sleep apnea and family history.
Look for signs of left-heart disease, lung disease and right-heart failure.
workup: Obtain ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography and cause-directed testing; PFTs, sleep evaluation, V/Q imaging or CT may be appropriate depending on suspected cause.
Right-heart catheterization is the definitive hemodynamic test when specialist evaluation indicates it.
management: Treat hypoxemia and underlying heart/lung disease appropriately and manage volume overload cautiously.
Refer suspected pulmonary arterial hypertension or chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension to an expert centre because therapy is classification- and hemodynamic-specific.
Pregnancy in significant pulmonary hypertension is high risk and requires urgent specialized cardio-obstetric/pulmonary input.
medicationSafety: Do not empirically start pulmonary vasodilator therapy before PH classification because some agents can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch or pulmonary edema in the wrong disease group.
Diuretics can relieve congestion but require renal/electrolyte monitoring and do not treat the pulmonary vascular cause.
redFlags: Resting hypoxemia or rapidly worsening dyspnea
Suspected chronic thromboembolic disease with decompensation
counselling: Explain that pulmonary hypertension is not one disease and that the cause determines therapy.
Advise urgent reassessment for syncope, chest pain, rapidly increasing edema or resting dyspnea.
followUp: Ensure closed-loop specialist referral and completion of the cause-classification workup.
Track functional status, oxygenation, volume status and right-heart findings while awaiting specialty care.
examTrap: Starting pulmonary arterial hypertension medication from an echocardiographic pressure estimate without confirming the PH group and hemodynamics.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a syndrome; classify the cause before treating the pulmonary vessels.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary vascular disease resources
CTS chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension guidance

title: Sarcoidosis: Multisystem Granulomatous Disease With Organ-Specific Risk
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis of compatible clinical/radiographic disease after important mimics are excluded, with tissue confirmation when needed. Treatment is driven by organ threat and functional impairment—not by an abnormal chest image alone.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, cough and dyspnea are common, but skin, eye, cardiac, neurologic, calcium and other organ involvement can dominate.
Some patients are asymptomatic and can be observed safely if organ-threatening disease is excluded.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, occupational exposures and other granulomatous diseases can mimic sarcoidosis.
Hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria, uveitis or conduction disease may be manifestations rather than unrelated problems.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms, fever/weight loss, skin lesions, visual symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, kidney-stone symptoms and relevant exposure/infection risks.
Perform cardiopulmonary, skin, eye-oriented and neurologic assessment according to symptoms.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary function testing to define thoracic disease and function.
Obtain tissue from the safest high-yield site when confirmation is needed and exclude infection/malignancy appropriately.
Screen for organ involvement with ECG and targeted calcium, renal, hepatic, ophthalmic or cardiac testing according to presentation and specialty guidance.
management: Observe selected stable asymptomatic disease without organ threat.
Use corticosteroids or steroid-sparing therapy when clinically significant pulmonary disease or organ-threatening extrapulmonary disease warrants treatment, usually with specialist involvement.
Cardiac, neurologic or vision-threatening disease requires expedited specialty care.
medicationSafety: Long-term corticosteroid therapy requires glucose, BP, bone, infection and other exposure-appropriate monitoring.
Do not start immunosuppression before reasonably excluding infections such as TB when the presentation/exposure risk makes them plausible.
redFlags: Syncope or conduction abnormality suggesting cardiac sarcoidosis
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can affect organs beyond the lungs and that symptoms such as syncope or visual change require prompt assessment.
Avoid excessive calcium/vitamin D supplementation without clinical review when hypercalcemia risk is present.
followUp: Track symptoms, PFTs/imaging when clinically useful and organ-specific complications.
Reassess treatment need rather than continuing corticosteroids indefinitely without a disease-control/toxicity plan.
examTrap: Treating every radiographic sarcoidosis finding with steroids or overlooking syncope as a clue to cardiac involvement.
oneLinePearl: In sarcoidosis, the treatment question is not 'is it present?' but 'is an organ threatened?'.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory specialty resources

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Chronic Multisystem Care and Exacerbation Recognition
bottomLine: Adults with cystic fibrosis require specialist multidisciplinary care that integrates airway clearance, chronic infection management, CFTR-modulator eligibility, nutrition/pancreatic disease, diabetes, liver/bone/reproductive health and rapid assessment of pulmonary exacerbations. Primary care should support—not duplicate or interrupt—the CF centre plan.
recognize: Increasing cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, weight loss and decline in lung function can signal pulmonary exacerbation.
CF-related diabetes, pancreatic insufficiency, liver disease, bone disease, sinus disease, fertility/reproductive issues and medication burden are common adult-care domains.
differentiate: Chronic airway colonization is expected in many patients; antibiotic choice for exacerbation is informed by the person's prior microbiology and specialist plan.
CFTR modulators are genotype- and product-specific therapies and require specialist eligibility/interaction monitoring.
assessment: Ask about deviation from personal respiratory baseline, sputum, hemoptysis, fever, exercise tolerance, weight/nutrition, airway-clearance adherence, CF medications, glucose issues and access to the CF centre.
Assess oxygenation and work of breathing and identify sepsis, major hemoptysis or pneumothorax signs urgently.
workup: Coordinate sputum microbiology and spirometry through the CF pathway during deterioration and use imaging/labs according to severity.
Maintain screening for CF-related diabetes, nutrition/vitamin status, liver/bone disease and other complications according to the CF centre plan.
management: Continue individualized airway clearance and chronic therapies unless the specialty/acute-care team advises otherwise.
Pulmonary exacerbations often require organism- and history-informed antibiotics and CF-centre coordination; severe disease may need hospital care.
Support vaccination, nutrition, exercise, reproductive planning and mental-health care as part of routine adult primary care.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators and chronic anti-infective regimens have major interaction/monitoring considerations; verify the current CF-centre/monograph plan before adding interacting drugs.
Pancreatic enzymes are taken with meals/snacks and require individualized dosing; do not replace specialty nutrition management with generic high-fibre/low-fat advice.
redFlags: New resting hypoxemia or respiratory failure
counselling: Encourage early contact with the CF team for respiratory deterioration rather than waiting for a routine visit.
Discuss fertility, pregnancy and medication planning proactively as survival into adulthood continues to improve.
followUp: Maintain shared care with an accredited CF centre and close loops on specialist monitoring.
Review adherence burden, mental health, access and transition issues because treatment complexity itself can drive morbidity.
examTrap: Treating a CF pulmonary exacerbation like ordinary community-acquired bronchitis without reviewing prior organisms or involving the CF team.
oneLinePearl: Adult CF is multisystem chronic disease; respiratory changes are managed against the patient's own microbiology and baseline.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Cystic Fibrosis working-group/education resources

title: Mechanical Ventilation: Read the Patient, Waveforms, Pressures, and Gas Exchange Together
bottomLine: Mechanical ventilation is supportive therapy, not a diagnosis. For an acutely ventilated patient, assess the patient first, then determine whether the problem is oxygenation, ventilation, airway/circuit mechanics, synchrony or hemodynamics. Sudden deterioration requires immediate bedside troubleshooting before changing complex ventilator settings by guesswork.
recognize: Hypoxemia relates to oxygen delivery/VQ/shunt/recruitment, while hypercapnia relates primarily to alveolar ventilation.
High peak pressure with unchanged plateau suggests increased airway resistance; rising plateau pressure suggests reduced respiratory-system compliance.
Patient-ventilator dyssynchrony can increase work of breathing, sedation exposure and injury risk.
differentiate: Ventilator alarm is a signal, not a diagnosis: secretions, biting/kinking, bronchospasm, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, derecruitment, circuit disconnection and patient agitation have different fixes.
A normal oxygen saturation does not prove adequate ventilation; CO2/pH and clinical status matter.
assessment: Assess airway position/patency, chest movement, breath sounds, oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental status/sedation and ventilator/circuit connection.
Review mode, set and delivered tidal volume, respiratory rate, FiO2, PEEP, peak/plateau pressures and recent ABG/VBG trends with the critical-care team.
workup: Use blood gases when gas exchange/acid-base status needs clarification and chest imaging for tube position or suspected pulmonary complication when indicated.
Trend mechanics and gas exchange after each intervention rather than making multiple simultaneous changes without reassessment.
management: In sudden severe desaturation or inability to ventilate, call for immediate critical-care/airway help and use a structured airway-breathing-circuit evaluation; manual ventilation may be required while the cause is identified.
Use lung-protective ventilation principles in ARDS/at-risk lungs and adjust oxygen/PEEP/ventilation targets under the active critical-care protocol.
Treat the underlying cause and minimize avoidable deep sedation/immobility when clinically safe.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, analgesics and neuromuscular blockers can cause hypotension, delirium, prolonged ventilation and awareness risk; use indication-based monitoring.
Do not treat dyssynchrony automatically with more sedation before checking pain, secretions, tube/circuit problems and ventilator settings.
redFlags: Sudden desaturation or loss of delivered volume
Absent unilateral breath sounds/tension pneumothorax concern
counselling: For families, explain that ventilator settings change as lung mechanics and gas exchange change; one number does not represent overall recovery.
followUp: Reassess readiness for spontaneous breathing/weaning when the cause improves and hemodynamics/oxygenation are suitable.
Use multidisciplinary ICU protocols for sedation, delirium prevention, mobilization and extubation readiness.
examTrap: Responding to a high-pressure alarm by changing ventilator settings before assessing the patient, airway and circuit.
oneLinePearl: Ventilator troubleshooting starts at the patient and airway, then moves to mechanics and settings.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society home/mechanical ventilation resources
Canadian critical-care lung-protective ventilation practice principles

title: Asthma-COPD Overlap: Preserve Asthma Safety While Treating COPD Burden
bottomLine: When a patient has persistent airflow obstruction plus convincing asthma features, preserve asthma-directed anti-inflammatory safety: inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy is required, while bronchodilator intensity and COPD prevention/rehabilitation are individualized to symptoms and exacerbation burden. Do not use LABA monotherapy in a patient with asthma features.
recognize: Asthma features include variable symptoms, atopy/early onset and variable airflow limitation; COPD features include persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction, exposure history and progressive exertional symptoms.
The overlap label is less important than identifying which treatable traits and medication-safety rules apply.
differentiate: Asthma alone can develop persistent obstruction, and COPD can show bronchodilator responsiveness; one spirometry change does not define overlap.
Eosinophilia may support an inflammatory phenotype but does not replace the clinical diagnosis.
assessment: Confirm inhaler technique/adherence, smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, symptom variability, exacerbations, atopy, eosinophil context, pneumonia history and comorbid rhinitis/OSA/GERD/cardiovascular disease.
workup: Use quality spirometry to document airflow limitation and bronchodilator response; reassess diagnosis when testing and clinical history conflict.
Use imaging or additional pulmonary testing only when alternative diagnoses are plausible.
management: Use an inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimen when asthma is present; add long-acting bronchodilation according to persistent obstruction, symptoms and exacerbation risk.
Provide smoking cessation, vaccination, exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation and individualized action planning.
Refer when diagnosis remains uncertain, exacerbations persist despite optimized therapy or severe asthma/COPD features are present.
medicationSafety: Avoid LABA monotherapy when asthma is part of the phenotype.
Balance ICS benefit against pneumonia/oral candidiasis/systemic exposure risk and use the lowest effective regimen consistent with asthma safety and exacerbation control.
Check inhaler device technique before escalating medication class.
redFlags: Hemoptysis/weight loss suggesting an alternate diagnosis
counselling: Explain that the treatment plan protects against asthma-related risk while also addressing fixed COPD symptoms/exacerbations.
Teach inhaler technique and a clear plan for worsening symptoms.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, rescue use, spirometry when clinically useful, adherence and adverse effects.
Step treatment based on objective control and risk rather than diagnostic label alone.
examTrap: Using LABA alone because spirometry looks like COPD despite a convincing asthma history.
oneLinePearl: If asthma is truly present, keep inhaled corticosteroid protection while treating the COPD traits around it.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD pharmacotherapy guidance
